items.abstract: <jats:p>The Team Orienteering Problem (TOP) maximizes collected reward under fleet and route-length limits. Direct-feasibility filtering can exclude a high-reward customer even when a bounded ejectionand-rearrangement move would yield a feasible net gain. We embed Ejection-Aware Repair in Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) to retain selected direct-infeasible candidates, rank removable customers by removal density, apply bounded 2-opt when needed, and commit only feasible positive-gain moves. Across 82 Dang benchmark instances, a paired four-seed ablation at 2,500 iterations reduced the average best-seed best-known-solution (BKS) gap from 3.707% to 1.820% and the average mean-seed gap from 4.998% to 3.038%. Ejection ON recorded 60/13/9 best-seed and 68/3/11 mean-seed wins/ties/losses against Ejection OFF. Mean wall-clock runtime per seed increased by 36.6%, to 68.857 s. Under a symmetric wall-clock ablation with time-based cooling, Ejection ON retained lower average best-seed and mean-seed gaps (1.822% and 2.937%) than Ejection OFF (3.260% and 4.501%). A supplementary instance-matched comparison retained the 1.820% fixed-iteration Ejection ON result as the reference. Five time-stopped comparators produced best-seed gaps from 3.561% to 18.618%, with all runs feasible and within budget. The logged nine-instance study recorded 77,390 successful commits. After averaging the two seeds within each instance, removal-density ranking yielded lower gaps in seven of nine blocks, but the Holmadjusted p-value was 0.6445. Bounded 2-opt participated in 18.2% of commits without a significant isolated instance-level effect.</jats:p>
